Then Islam (al-Islamiyya), which is the soundest of them all and the furthest from distortion and alteration. Likewise, Islam began with gentleness and pardon, and then with firmness and punishment. It is not hidden from researchers that there is a great resemblance between Buddha and Jesus and their religions, and likewise between Moses and Muhammad and their religions. Therefore the first two were joined together and the latter two likewise. He placed Buddhism before Christianity because of the antiquity of the former, just as He placed Mosaism (al-Musawiyya) before Muhammadanism (al-Muhammadiyya) for this very same reason.

Among the excellent features of the verse also is the symbolism and allusion to the two religions of mercy by the fig and the olive, and to the two religions of justice by the mountain and the mountainous town, Mecca, which is the secure city (al-balad al-amin). Among the wonderful harmony between the words of the verse is that the fig and the olive grow abundantly in the valleys of mountains, as in the Mount of Olives in Syria (al-Sham) and Mount Sinai (Tur Sina'), and both are famous there.

(p-6201) This verse is therefore an oath by the first places of the descent of revelation, and by the most noble places of the divine manifestation upon His four prophets, whose laws have remained until now, whom God sent to guide people, whom He created in the best of forms. The end of his words verbatim. And God knows best.

A subtle point (lata'if):
"Sinin" is not declined (lam yanṣarif), just as "Sina'" is not declined, because it has been made a name for a locality or land, so it is a non-Arabic proper noun (ʿalam a'jami). But if it had been made a name for a place or a dwelling, or a name for a male, it would be declined, because you named a male with it. The common reading (al-'amma) is "Sinin" with a kasra on the sin, and some of the early generation (al-salaf) read it with a fatha, and others read "Sina'" with a kasra and a fatha, with the long vowel. Al-Samin said: These are dialects that differed regarding this Syriac name, following the habit of the Arabs in playing with non-Arabic names.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 95, verses 4–8:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[4–8] ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature.﴾ ﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low.﴾ [At-Tin: 5] ﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds, for they will have a reward uninterrupted.﴾ [At-Tin: 6] ﴿So what causes you to deny the Recompense after [this]?﴾ [At-Tin: 7] ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [At-Tin: 8]

As for His words, ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature﴾: that is, in the best of proportion, in form and shape, in appearance and meaning. Al-Shihab said: The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "man." Al-taqwim (the act of making upright and proportionate) is an action of Allah, so it has the meaning of al-qawwam (the one who establishes) or al-muqawwim (the one who makes upright). Or there is an implied noun governed by it, meaning "a most excellent upright form (qiwam)." Or "fi" is redundant, and the implied sense is: "We made him upright in the best manner."

﴿Then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [At-Tin: 5]: that is, We made him lower than any lowness, namely the people of the Fire, because he did not act according to what We created him upon of the attributes which, had he acted in accordance with them, would have placed him in the highest of the high (ʿIlliyyin). Thus "radda" (returned) here carries the meaning of "ja'ala" (made), which takes two objects. Al-Shihab said: "Al-safilin" refers to the disobedient and others, and "asfal safil" is for a plural that varies in degree. "Thumma" (then) indicates either temporal sequence or rank. It is permissible to read "asfala" as accusative by removing the preposition, as a qualifier of an omitted noun, meaning: "to a place lower than the lowest," that is, the place of the Fire, or the Fire in the sense of Jahannam. This is what Mujahid said when he stated, "In the Fire," and in another narration, "To the Fire." The "lowest" would then refer to the lowest places, which are its levels (darakat). Its plural form for rational beings is for the sake of the verse-ending (fasila), or by treating them as rational beings. Thus they said. But if what is meant is the people of the Fire and its levels, since they are the lowest of the low, as in the first interpretation, it would be more appropriate.

﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds, for they will have a reward uninterrupted﴾ [At-Tin: 6]: that is, not cut off, or not diminished, or not counted, or not bestowed upon them with obligation. The exception is a continuous (muttasil) exception from the pronoun in "radadnahu," since it has the sense of a plural, because the one referred to, man, has the sense of a genus.

Ibn Jarir relied, in interpreting the verse, on what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: that the meaning is, "Then We returned him to the most miserable age." And that whoever used to act in obedience to Allah throughout his youth, then grew old until his intellect departed, would have recorded for him the like of his righteous deeds which he used to do in his youth, and he would not be held accountable for anything he did in his old age and the loss of his intellect, because he was a believer and used to obey Allah in his youth.

Ibn Jarir's words: "The most correct of the statements in this regard, in my view, and the most similar to the interpretation of the verse, is the statement of the one who said its meaning is: 'Then We returned him,' that is, to the most miserable age, to the age of senility of those whose intellects have departed due to decrepitude and old age. He is thus in the lowest of the low in the decline of life and the loss of intellect."

﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [At-Tin: 6]: in their state of health and youth, ﴿for them is a reward uninterrupted﴾ [At-Tin: 6] after their decrepitude, like the likeness of what they had of that in their deeds, in the state in which they used to act while they were strong upon the work.

He said: We only said this is the more correct view in this matter because Allah, exalted is His remembrance, informed about His creation of the son of Adam and His alternation of his states, as a proof against those who deny His power to resurrect after death. Do you not see that He says: ﴿So what causes you to deny the Recompense after [this]?﴾ [At-Tin: 7], meaning after these proofs. It is impossible that He would argue against a people who deny a matter by means of what they deny. Rather, the proof against every people is by what they cannot repel of what they witness and perceive, or what they acknowledge even if they were not perceiving it. Since that is so, and since those people denied the Fire with which Allah threatened them in the Hereafter, while they had witnessed the people of decrepitude and senility after youth and vigor, He knew that He was only arguing against them by what they had witnessed of His alternation of creation and His transfer of them from the state of good proportion, youth and vigor, to decrepitude, weakness, the end of life, and the onset of senility. End of his words.

Accordingly, the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), serving as a correction to dispel the assumption that equality in the most miserable age entails equality in other respects. In that case, "al-din" (the Recompense) is a subject (mubtada'), and the "fa'" enters upon its predicate. As for the first interpretation, the "fa'" is for consequence, and what follows it is a sentence that is a consequence of it and reinforces it.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿So what causes you to deny the Recompense after [this]?﴾ [At-Tin: 7], are an address to man by way of iltifat (shift of address), to intensify the rebuke and reproach, that is: What moves you to deny the Recompense, that is, the requital after resurrection, and to reject it after these proofs?

The meaning is: the creation of man from a drop of semen, his formation as a complete human, and his transformation from state to state, in perfection and deficiency, are among the clearest proofs of the power of Allah, mighty and majestic, to resurrect and to recompense. So what compels you to deny it?

It is also permissible that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the meaning of "yukadhdhibuka" is either that it attributes to you falsehood (like "fassaqtuhu" when you say to him, "You are a sinner"), and the "ba'" in "bil-din" carries the sense of "fi" (concerning), that is: he denies you in your report about it; or it is causative, that is: because of your report of it and affirmation of it; or the meaning is: what makes you a denier of the Recompense, with the "ba'" being its complement. This is of the manner of stirring and indirect reference to the deniers: the meaning is that nothing will make you deny the Recompense after this clarification, unlike those who do not care for the signs of Allah and do not raise their heads to them. The interrogation is for denial and wonder.

Ibn Jarir preferred the view of those who said: "ma" means "man," that is: "Then who will deny you, O Muhammad, after what has come to you of this clarification from Allah concerning the Recompense?"

Al-Shihab said: "Fa-ma" is an interrogative about one who has intellect, and this is open to scrutiny, because it contradicts what is known; it should not be resorted to while its retention in its original sense is sound, as we have explained to you. The motive for resorting to this is that the meaning is clearer on it when the addressee is the Prophet ﷺ; for it is a rebuking denial of those who deny him ﷺ after the proofs of his truthfulness and the soundness of his claim have become apparent to them.

﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [At-Tin: 8]: that is, the most just of those who judge in their judgments. Abu al-Su'ud said: That is: Is not He who did what was mentioned the most just of judges in His craftsmanship and management, such that one might suppose the non-occurrence of re-creation and recompense? And since it is impossible that He is not the most just of judges, re-creation and recompense are established. So the sentence serves as confirmation of what precedes it. It was said: "Al-hukm" means judgment (qada'), so it is a warning to the disbelievers that He will judge them by what they deserve of punishment. And "ahkam" is from "al-hukm" or "al-hikmah" (wisdom). It was said: The second is more apparent.

It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ, when he recited it, would say: "Yes, and I am among the witnesses to that." Qatadah transmitted it as a mursal report, and Abu Hurayrah traced it to the Prophet ﷺ.

The meaning is: the creation of man from a drop of semen, his formation as a complete human, and his transformation from state to state, in perfection and deficiency, are among the clearest proofs of the power of Allah, mighty and majestic, to resurrect and to recompense. So what compels you to deny it?

It is also permissible that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the meaning of "yukadhdhibuka" is either that it attributes to you falsehood (like "fassaqtuhu" when you say to him, "You are a sinner"), and the "ba'" in "bil-din" carries the sense of "fi" (concerning), that is: he denies you in your report about it; or it is causative, that is: because of your report of it and affirmation of it; or the meaning is: what makes you a denier of the Recompense, with the "ba'" being its complement. This is of the manner of stirring and indirect reference to the deniers: the meaning is that nothing will make you deny the Recompense after this clarification, unlike those who do not care for the signs of Allah and do not raise their heads to them. The interrogation is for denial and wonder.

Ibn Jarir preferred the view of those who said: "ma" means "man," that is: "Then who will deny you, O Muhammad, after what has come to you of this clarification from Allah concerning the Recompense?"

Al-Shihab said: "Fa-ma" is an interrogative about one who has intellect, and this is open to scrutiny, because it contradicts what is known; it should not be resorted to while its retention in its original sense is sound, as we have explained to you. The motive for resorting to this is that the meaning is clearer on it when the addressee is the Prophet ﷺ; for it is a rebuking denial of those who deny him ﷺ after the proofs of his truthfulness and the soundness of his claim have become apparent to them.

﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [At-Tin: 8]: that is, the most just of those who judge in their judgments. Abu al-Su'ud said: That is: Is not He who did what was mentioned the most just of judges in His craftsmanship and management, such that one might suppose the non-occurrence of re-creation and recompense? And since it is impossible that He is not the most just of judges, re-creation and recompense are established. So the sentence serves as confirmation of what precedes it. It was said: "Al-hukm" means judgment (qada'), so it is a warning to the disbelievers that He will judge them by what they deserve of punishment. And "ahkam" is from "al-hukm" or "al-hikmah" (wisdom). It was said: The second is more apparent.

It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ, when he recited it, would say: "Yes, and I am among the witnesses to that." Qatadah transmitted it as a mursal report, and Abu Hurayrah traced it to the Prophet ﷺ.
